en: The Explanation of the Chief Mañjuvajra; Homage to Śrī Vajrasattva.

I pay homage to the body of the Victors— liberated from the conduct of the three worlds, situated like space, the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, pure, peaceful, secluded, consisting of supreme bliss, accessible only to yogins, difficult to understand, difficult to analyze, the greatest benefit for oneself and others, pervasive, definitive, blissful, peerless, and the singular embodiment of non-conceptuality.
Having uttered "Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ," one should visualize a blue syllable *Hūṃ* upon a sun disk at one's own heart; having beautified all limbs with rays of light shaped like Indra’s bow, one recites:
"Oṃ, all phenomena are pure through yoga; I am pure through yoga."
Having visualized the syllable ĀḤ at the throat, illuminating the entire body with red rays, one should contemplate the indestructible body of a diamond (vajra) the color of a mani-gem.
Reciting: "Oṃ, all phenomena are pure as a diamond; I am pure as a diamond," and having meditated on the syllable Oṃ at the head, [one should contemplate] all [beings] with white-colored rays.
Having purified the body, one should meditate upon it as resembling pure crystal:
*Oṃ śubhāvaśuddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ śubhāvaśuddho ’ham*.
Thereafter, having visualized within the heart a white five-pronged vajra the size of a barley grain.
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the selflessness of all phenomena; for the sake of upholding all sentient beings, I am of the nature of Mañjuvajra.
The purification of the hands.
In the right hand, by means of the syllable *āḥ*, there is a sun-maṇḍala with the syllables *bruṃ āṃ jrīṃ khaṃ hūṃ*.
In the left hand, by means of the syllable *aḥ*, there is a moon-maṇḍala with the syllables *lāṃ māṃ pāṃ tāṃ oṃ*.
This is the consecration of the lotus-turning conch.
Oṃ maṃ Mañjuvajra hūṃ | Oṃ Vighnāntakṛt hūṃ | Oṃ sarvavighnān utsāraya hūṃ |
The offering of the consecrated flower for the protection of the site begins with "Oṃ Akāramukha" and so forth.
Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ: the consecration of the maṇḍala.
(1) Oṃ. Homage to Mañjuvajra.
"Released from the conduct of the three worlds," and so forth.
Thus it was said.
Having purified all limbs with rays in the shape of a rainbow from the blue syllable *hūṃ* in the sun [disk] at one's own heart;
Oṃ, all phenomena are pure through yoga; I am pure through yoga.
Having visualized the body as the color of ruby, with a vajra-like indestructible form, one illuminates the entire body from the syllable ĀḤ at the throat by means of its red rays of light.
Oṃ, all phenomena are pure like a vajra; I am pure like a vajra.
Having meditated on the syllable Oṃ at the head, white in color, one should purify the entire body with its rays of light and contemplate it as resembling pure crystal.
Oṃ, all phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature.
Thereafter, having visualized within one's own heart a white five-pronged vajra the size of a barley grain.
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the selflessness of all phenomena.
For the sake of upholding all sentient beings, I am of the very nature of Mañjuvajra.
Following that is the purification of the hands.
It is like the sequence of the *piṇḍa*.
The seat of Śaṅkha.
Oṃ Mañjuvajra Hūṃ.
Oṃ, O destroyer of obstacles, hūṃ!
Oṃ, drive away all obstacles, hūṃ!
The sprinkling mantra.
Oṃ, the syllable *a* is the mouth, and so forth.
Bali.
Oṃ āḥ hūṃ. Purification of the maṇḍala by means of mantra. (2)
"Protect my place," and so forth.
Then one should cultivate loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.

Following that, one should visualize a syllable *hūṃ* upon a sun disk at one’s own heart, produced from the letter *ra*; through its transformation, one should cultivate the ego-identity of Dveṣavajra.

He is blue in color, six-armed, and stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture with three faces: the right [face] is red and the left is white. He is embraced by his consort, who has the same appearance as himself. With his first two hands he holds a vajra and a vajra-bell; with the second pair, a sword and a noose with the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*).

With the third two [hands], one should meditate upon the wheel and skull-staff, sealed with the *khaṃ* syllable, adorned with a garland of human heads, with tawny hair standing erect, three eyes, frowning brows, and lips smeared [with blood], terrifying, possessing the splendor of the fire of universal destruction, treading upon Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, and manifesting the *vajra-hūṃkāra*.

Then, from the syllable *bhrūṃ* in the sky, one should emanate a yellow ten-spoked wheel; upon its spokes, one should project Yamāntaka and the other [deities], arisen from *hūṃ* syllables within oceans of light, standing in the pratyālīḍha posture.
Oṃ śumbha niśumbha, and so forth.
Then, with rays of light from the syllable *hūṃ*, one should visualize a vajra ground, a vajra fence, a vajra canopy, and a net of vajra arrows.
Having summoned the hosts of obstructors into the pits near the fence, one should nail them down.
Oṃ gha gha ghāṭaya 2 sarvaduṣṭetyādi.
One should contemplate it as being free from obstacles.

Within one's own heart, by means of the syllable *A*, there is a moon; above that is the syllable *Maṃ*. By its rays of light, having gone to the Kāñcanamaṇḍala world-system, one draws forth the Mañjuvajra maṇḍala.
Oṃ, [homage] to Vajrāṅkuśa and the others.
Oṃ āḥ Mañjuvajra, for the venerable Lord, [I offer] water for the face, water for the feet, water for sipping, and water for sprinkling.
jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ.
Oṃ āḥ maṃ Mañjuvajra hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ āḥ Dharmadhātuvajra hūṃ | Oṃ Jinajika hūṃ |
Oṃ Ratnadhṛka trāṃ | Oṃ Ārolika hrīḥ | Oṃ Prajñādhṛka khaṃ |
Oṃ, Oṃ Moharate Lāṃ; Oṃ, Oṃ Dveṣarate Māṃ; Oṃ, Oṃ Rāgarate Pāṃ.
Oṃ vajrarate trāṃ | Oṃ rūpavajre ja hūṃ | Oṃ śabdavajre hūṃ |
Oṃ oṃ gandhavajre vaṃ hūṃ | Oṃ rasavajre ho hūṃ | (3) The purification of the mantras is as in the Piṇḍakrama.
Oṃ, protect my non-abiding! Hūṃ, and so forth.
Then one should cultivate loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity.
Following that, from the syllable *repha* at one’s own heart, upon a sun disk, through the transformation of the syllable *hūṃ*, one should cultivate the pride of Dveṣavajra.
He is blue in color, has six arms, and stands in the pratyālīḍha posture with three faces—the right red and the left white—and is embraced by his consort, who is of the same appearance as himself.
With his first two hands he holds a vajra and a vajra-bell; with the second pair, a sword and a noose with the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*); and with the third pair, a wheel and a *khaṭvāṅga*.

He wears a garland of human heads and a crown of skulls, has hair standing erect and upward-pointing, three eyes, and a frowning brow. Terrifying and fierce toward the wicked, he possesses the splendor of the fire of cosmic destruction and stands treading upon Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa. This is Vajra-Hūṃkāra.
One should meditate.

Then, in the sky, by means of the syllable *Bhrūṃ*, one should expand a yellow ten-spoked wheel; upon its spokes, one should manifest Yamāntaka and the others, standing upon sun discs arisen from the syllable *Hūṃ*, in the *pratyālidha* posture, and cause them to radiate forth.
Oṃ suṃbha niḥsuṃbha, and so forth.
Then, with rays of light from the syllable *hūṃ*, one should cause a vajra-ground, a vajra-fence, a vajra-canopy, and a network of vajra-arrows to descend.
Near the enclosure, at the corners,
[one should place] the obstructing spirits (*vighna*).
Having brought them, one should play with them.
Oṃ gha gha ghāṭaya 2 sarvaduṣṭa, etc.
One should meditate without obstacles.
By means of the syllable *A* in one's own heart, [one visualizes] a moon disc; above that, the syllable *Maṃ*.
By its light rays, having gone to the world-realm of Kāñcanī, one draws forth the Mañjuvajra maṇḍala.
Oṃ, [the mantra] beginning with Vajrāṅkuśa.
Oṃ āḥ, to the venerable Mañjuvajra, [I offer] water for the face, water for the feet, water for sipping, and water for purification; please accept it, svāhā!
jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ
Oṃ āḥ maṃ Mañjuvajra hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ āḥ Dharmadhātuvajra hūṃ ||
Oṃ jinajika hūṃ | Oṃ ratnadhṛka trāṃ | Oṃ āḥ rolika hrīṃḥ |
Oṃ, Khaṃ, the holder of wisdom.
Oṃ, O you who delight in delusion, protect me! Oṃ, O you who delight in hatred, protect her! Oṃ, O you who delight in passion, protect him!
Oṃ vajrarate tāṃ | Oṃ rūpavajre ja hūṃ ||
Oṃ Śabdavajre hūṃ.
Oṃ gandhavajre vaṃ hūṃ.
Oṃ rasavajre ho hūṃ | (4) sparśavajre hūṃ | Oṃ dharmadhātuvajre hūṃ |
Oṃ Yamāntaka hūṃ | Oṃ Prajñāntaka hūṃ | Oṃ Padmāntaka hūṃ |
Oṃ vighnāntaka hūṃ | Oṃ vajrāyudhe svāhā | Oṃ vajrakālāya svāhā ||
Oṃ, svāhā to the Nāga-vajra!
Oṃ vajrabhairavāya svāhā | Oṃ vajrānalāya svāhā | Oṃ vajrarākṣasāya svāhā |
Oṃ, svāhā to Vajrānila! Oṃ, svāhā to Vajrakrodha!
Oṃ, svāhā to Vajrakuṇḍalin!
Oṃ vajraprabha svāhā.
Oṃ maunavajrāya svāhā | Oṃ vemacitrine svāhā ||
Oṃ, svāhā to the Earth!
Oṃ, svāhā to the serpent Śeṣa!
The five-fold offering, the eight [mudrās], the sounding of the bell, and the hymn of praise.
"Akṣobhyavajra," and so forth.
By means of the three mantras.

I bow to the fivefold form: the radiant image of the Buddha, the bearer of the sun’s rays; Maitreya of lovely form, marked with the streaks of the moon’s essence; the beautiful-bodied Mañjughoṣa upon the head; the staff-bearing form arising from the lotus, whose body is adorned with skin; the terrible state of the Vajra-holder; Sound, Consciousness, and the form of primordial wisdom who has cast away the fear of existence.
Confession of Evil Deeds.
Whatever beginningless stream of existence has been fashioned as entirely conceptual and defiled,
I confess all of that in its entirety according to the rule before those of great compassion.
Having rejoiced in all the merit performed by the perfectly awakened ones, the bodhisattvas, the noble ones, and others, I correctly dedicate it in its entirety toward perfect enlightenment.
I go for refuge to the Sugata, whose infinite and noble means of compassion are purified by the shining full moon of his mind,

who does not return to saṃsāra, and who is eternally free from all conceptual construction. I go for refuge to the Dharma, the support of the prosperity of all virtuous beings, whose nature is the single flavor of all phenomena.

I have gone for refuge to that supreme bed of the ascetics, which has completely cast off all bonds, which possesses the glory bestowed by the highest compassion, which has entered the stages beginning with *muditā*,
and which has been produced through the purification of intention and the maturation [of merit], thereby destroying all obscurations.

I generate the resolve for awakening, adorned with resolute conviction; I have now taken refuge in the Sugata, the path of the Sugatas, which consists of the ten kinds of pure qualities such as generosity, and in the Buddhas who perceive all phenomena as being of the nature of perfect enlightenment.
(5) Oṃ kharasavajre hūṃ.
Oṃ dharmadhātuvajre hūṃ.
Oṃ Yamāntaka hūṃ.
Oṃ Prajñāntaka Hūṃ.
Oṃ Vighnāntakṛ Hūṃ.
Oṃ vajrayuddha svāhā.
Oṃ, svāhā to the one who performs the vajra-action!
Oṃ, svāhā to the Nāga-vajra!
Oṃ, svāhā to Vajrabhairava!
Oṃ vajrānarāya svāhā.
Oṃ, svāhā to the one with adamantine eyes!
Oṃ, svāhā to Vajranīla!
Oṃ, svāhā to the Vajra Wrathful One!
Oṃ vajrakuṇḍalīne svāhā.
Oṃ vajraprabhāya svāhā.
Oṃ, svāhā to Maunavajrā!
Oṃ, to Vemacitrin, svāhā!
Oṃ, to the earth, svāhā!
Oṃ, svāhā to Seṣanāga!
Paṃ aṣṭau lā ghaṃ stu.
Oṃ Akṣobhyavajra, and so forth.
Established therein.
Confession of Evil Deeds.
"Or else, in beginningless existence," and so forth.
(6) Having taken hold of this world of sentient beings, which is ensnared by the net of views, one who possesses wisdom and mantras should, out of compassion,
generate the incomparable mind of complete enlightenment and become a practitioner.
Thus ends the introductory yoga.
Immediately after that: "In the absence [of intrinsic nature], there is no cultivation of existence; the non-cultivation of existence is not cultivation at all.
Thus, because of existence, the cultivation of existence is not perceived.
By means of this, one should cause [the practitioner] to enter into emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Then, from the syllable *yaṃ*, the wind mandala [arises] within the void; from the syllable *raṃ*, the fire mandala; from the syllable *vaṃ*, the water mandala;
and from the syllable *laṃ*, the earth mandala.

Through the dissolution of these four mandalas, there arises the vajra ground. In its center, from the syllable *bhrūṃ*, arises the peaked temple (*kūṭāṅgāra*), square with four doors, adorned with eight pillars, and featuring necklaces, half-necklaces, and a pinnacle of stepped tiers.

Above that is a universal lotus; above that, from the syllable *maṃ*, one should visualize Mañjuvajra with three faces and six arms: the central face is reddish-brown like saffron, the right is blue, and the left is white.
One should cause Vairocana and the other deities of the maṇḍala to enter into one’s own body.
Oṃ āḥ hūṃ svāhā.
In the head, throat, heart, navel, and both feet.

Vairocana and the others follow in due order: the mirror-like [wisdom] resides in the aggregate of form; the earth element, the eye faculty, and form as the fifth proceed together with the wrathful [deity] and Maitreya.
The equality of the aggregate of sensation, the faculty of hearing, and sound as the fifth—these proceed together with the two types of wrath.
Volitional formations, the performance of actions, the wind-energy, the faculty of taste, and taste as the fifth—these proceed together with the two types of wrath.
The upper half, joined with wrath and appearing according to its own nature,
enters the aggregate of consciousness, and consciousness is luminous.
Nirvāṇa and universal emptiness are declared to be the Dharmakāya.
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the knowledge of emptiness.

Thereafter, one should contemplate in the sky a *hūṃ* and a sun-maṇḍala; above that, an *oṃ* and a moon-maṇḍala; and above that, an eight-petaled red lotus born from the syllable *āḥ*. Upon the lotus, one should visualize the three-syllable mantra. Immediately following that, [one should reflect]: "Meditation on non-existence is not meditation; indeed, there is no meditation that is not meditation. Thus, one does not undertake the meditation of existence or non-existence. By this, one should enter into emptiness.

Then, when it has become empty, from the syllable *yaṃ* arises a wind mandala; from the syllable *raṃ*, a fire mandala; from the syllable *vaṃ*, a water mandala; and from the syllable *laṃ*, an earth mandala.

Through the dissolution of these four mandalas, there appears a ground made of vajra. In its center, from the syllable *bhrūṃ*, arises a peaked temple (*kūṭāṅgāra*) that is square, with four doors, adorned with eight pillars, and decorated with necklaces (*hāra*), half-necklaces (*arddhahāra*), strings of pearls (*bakulika*), and garlands of flowers (*mālāśīrṣaka*).

Above that, upon a double lotus, one should meditate on Mañjuvajra produced from the syllable *maṃ*; he has three faces and six arms, with the central face red like saffron, the right blue, and the left white, joined with Prajñā.
One should then cause Vairocana and the other deities of the maṇḍala to enter into one’s own body.
Oṃ āḥ hūṃ svāhā.
[Place them] on the head, throat, heart, navel, and the two feet.
Vairocana and the others follow in due order: the aggregate of form consists of the mirror-like wisdom, the earth element, the eye faculty,
and the fifth, visible form, which proceeds in union with the wrathful and loving ones.
The equality of the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha), the element of water (āpa-dhātu), the faculty of hearing, and sound as the fifth—these proceed together with the two types of anger.
The formative forces (saṃskāra) are the performance of duties, the wind element (māruta), and the faculty of taste.
And the fifth is Śara, accompanied by the two Krodhas.
The upper half, joined with wrath and appearing according to its own nature, becomes the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*); thus consciousness itself is the fivefold luminosity.
Nirvāṇa and universal emptiness are declared to be the Dharmakāya.
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness.
Thereafter, one should contemplate in space the syllable *hūṃ* as a sun-maṇḍala; above that, the syllable *oṃ* as a moon-maṇḍala; and above that, a red *ādarapadma* born from the syllable *ā*.
Upon the lotus, one should meditate on the *trekṣala* mantra. One should then visualize the mantra, the lotus, and the sun entering into the moon-maṇḍala, until only the moon-maṇḍala remains.
Then: "I am of the nature of the Dharmadhātu-vajra."
Then again, one should visualize a moon mandala with the syllables Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ.
Thereafter, having meditated upon white Vajrasattva arisen from those three syllables,
one should cause him to enter into Akṣobhya.
Then follows the ritual placement (nyāsa).

At the head is Vairocana, the aggregate of form, Locanā and so forth, the earth element, and the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). At the mouth is ĀḤ, Amitābha, the aggregate of perception, Pāṇḍarā, the fire element, and the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*). At the heart is HŪṂ, Akṣobhya, the aggregate of consciousness, the space element, and the wisdom of utter purity (*suviśuddhajñāna*). At the navel is SVĀ, Ratnasambhava, the aggregate of feeling, Māmakī, the water element, and the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*).
In the two feet: HĀ, Amoghasiddhi, the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha), Tārā, the wind element, and the all-accomplishing gnosis (kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna).
Oṃ rūpavajre hūṃ | Oṃ śabdavajre hūṃ | Oṃ gandhavajre hūṃ |
Oṃ raśavajre hūṃ | Oṃ sparśavajre hūṃ | Oṃ dharmadhātuvajre hūṃ |
Oṃ Yamāntaka hūṃ | Oṃ Prajñāntaka hūṃ | Oṃ Padmāntaka hūṃ | Oṃ Vighnāntaka hūṃ |
Then, in the center of the four mandalas upon the crown of the head, one should radiate the syllable Oṃ with five-colored rays of light: "Oṃ!
May the glorious holders of the Buddha-body, who are meditated upon as indivisible from the three vajras, grant me today the empowerment of the state of the Vajra Body."
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra body of all the Tathāgatas.
The glorious Dharma is indeed the path of speech, realized as the indivisibility of the three vajras.
May the Vajra-speech holders grant me today the consecration of that state!
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the speech-vajra of all the Tathāgatas.
O glorious Vajradhara, whose mind is the nature of mind and who is cultivated as the indivisible triple-vajra— may you,
the holders of the mind-vajra, today grant me the empowerment and the state of realization.
(9) Likewise, one should visualize the mantra-syllables as having entered the sun and become merely the size of the lunar disc.
Then: Oṃ, I am of the nature of the dharmadhātu.
Thereafter, one should again visualize a moon mandala with Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ.
Then, having visualized Vajrasattva, white in color and arisen from the three syllables,
one should cause him to enter the eyes.
Then, the entrustment.

Śīlaśrī is Vairocana, the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), Rocanā and so forth, the earth element (pṛthvīdhātu), and the mirror-like gnosis (ādarśajñāna); at the mouth is ĀḤ, Amitābha, the aggregate of perception (saṃjñāskandha), Pāṇḍarā, the fire element (tejodhātu), and the gnosis of equality (samatājñāna).
At the heart is HŪṂ, Akṣobhya, the aggregate of consciousness, the wisdom that is the utter purity of the space element. At the navel is SVĀ, Ratnasambhava, the aggregate of sensation.
Māmakī is the wisdom of discernment (pratyavekṣaṇājñāna) regarding the impure elements.
The two feet are Amoghasiddhi, the aggregate of formations; Tārā is the wind element and the all-accomplishing gnosis.
Oṃ rūpavajre hūṃ.
Oṃ śabdavajre hūṃ | Oṃ gandhavajre hūṃ ||
Oṃ rasavajre hoḥ | Oṃ rpaśyavajre hūṃ | Oṃ dharmadhātuvajre hūṃ |
Oṃ Yamāntaka hūṃ.
Oṃ Prajñāntaka Hūṃ.
Oṃ Padmāntaka Hūṃ.
Oṃ, you who bring an end to obstacles, hūṃ!
Then, in the center of a moon disc upon one's head, one should cause the syllable Oṃ to radiate five-colored rays of light.

Oṃ! May the glorious ones of the Buddha-body, who are meditated upon as indivisible from the three vajras, grant me today the empowerment and the state of the Vajra Body. Oṃ! I am of the nature of the Vajra Body of all Tathāgatas.
The glorious Dharma is the path of liberation, cultivated through the indivisibility of the three vajras.
May the wielders of the thunderbolt bestow upon me today their empowerment and their station.
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the speech-vajra of all the Tathāgatas.
O glorious holder of the mind-vajra, who possesses the indivisible nature of the three vajras,
may you today bestow upon me the empowerment and the state of the Mind-Vajra-holder.
(10) Then, one should visualize oneself as abiding within the four mandalas.
Equipped with a sword, wheel, lotus, and vajra,
one should meditate on the syllable *maṃ* within the fist of the sword at the heart of the Subtle Wisdom-Being (*sūkṣmajñānasattva*) in the center of the chest.
Then: HŪṂ VAJRA.
In the center is the sun.
OṂ; a lotus born from the form of the Goddess, with the letter JA as its filaments and PHAṬ in the opening.
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra that impassions all Tathāgatas.
HŪṂ 3 CĀLANAṂ | At the end: PHAṬ OṂ SARVATATHĀGATAPŪJĀVAJRASVABHĀVĀTMAKO ’HAṂ ||
Then, having produced one's own body, perfected from the syllables of one's own mantra,
one should manifest oneself as Mañjuvajra in the center of the lotus.
Then, having emanated from the heart the syllable *vaṃ*,
one should [visualize] the sword from the moon of the syllable *a*.
The Khaḍgamoṣṭa [deity] is the syllable Maṃ, red as saffron, produced from the syllable Maṃ; he has three faces, holds a sword in his hand, and is embraced by a consort of his own radiance;
his right and left faces are blue and white, respectively.
In his right hand he holds a sword and an arrow;
in his left hand, indeed, he holds a blue lotus.

One should visualize [himself] as Mañjuvajra, adorned with Akṣobhya, wearing a jeweled crown, seated in the vajra-posture upon a moon-disc seat, radiant with moonlight, and embellished with jewel ornaments, together with his own consort Prajñā.
One should visualize [the deities] beginning with Jinajik and ending with Vighnāntaka, possessing the aforementioned faces and arms.
Having drawn forth the gnosis-being (jñānasattva) by means of the rays from the seed-syllable in one's own heart.
For as it is said: "Just as, merely having gone," and so forth.
The consecrations; as before, the invocation; the offering of water for honor (*argha*) and so forth, and the ritual placement of flowers (*puṣpanyāsa*).
The graceful dance.
Praise of the Bell-Bearer (Ghaṇṭāvādāna-stuti)
Tarpaṇa (the ritual libation)
Following that is Mahāyoga.
The knower of yoga should always diligently meditate on a mustard seed at the tip of the nose, and within that mustard seed, the world with its moving and unmoving beings;
he should meditate on the form of suchness.
Thereafter, he should awaken the four goddesses.
O Vajra-mind, Lord of the World, protect me, O delightful being who desires the great purpose! Love me, O progenitor-being, O great supreme kinsman!
(11) Then, one should visualize oneself as situated within the four mandalas.

The sword-wheel joined with the lotus and vajra is at the center of the heart; O subtle wisdom, having meditated on the syllable *maṃ* within the heart, in the grip of the sword of all those [beings].
Then, *hūṃ* is the vajra in the center; *oṃ*, the sun;
*oṃ*, the lotus born from the letter *ā* of the Goddess; *ña-kāla*, the filaments; *randhre phaṭ*.
*Oṃ*, I am of the nature of the Vajra of Passion (*anurāgaṇa*) of all the Tathāgatas.
Hūṃ 3, the stirring.
Ante phaṭ!

If there is any turbidity born of all the conceptual constructions within the flood of existence that has no beginning, I confess it all according to the rule before those of great compassion.

Having rejoiced in whatever merit has been performed by the Perfect Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and other Noble Ones, I fully dedicate it all to the Perfect Buddhas, who possess radiant selves and whose infinite, pure compassion and skillful means are like the stainless moon.
I go for refuge to the Sugatas, who abide eternally within themselves;
I go for refuge to the Dharma, which is free from all remnants of conceptual construction, the basis for the excellence of true beings, and whose single nature pervades all things.
I have gone for refuge to the assembly of ascetics, who have completely cast off all bonds, who are graced with the splendor of supreme compassion,

and who have entered the stages beginning with *muditā* (joy). Through the purification of my intention and its maturation, having utterly eradicated all obscurations and habitual tendencies, I generate a mind adorned with devotion toward enlightenment.
